comments.author: @whythesenotes-adventuresin5576
comments.text:
Knowledge Distillation is a rather old concept in machine learning. I first remember coming across it years ago with optical character recognition. Train a model to recognize handwriting that’s very accurate, but very computationally expensive. Then train another model using the same input values, but the output of the model rather than the output of the raw data, and you get a model that’s nearly as accurate but much smaller.

So - hardly a “let the cat out of the bag” moment if you’ve been following machine learning for long enough….

These models are characterized by their ability to reason step-by-step, explore solution spaces, and perform complex tasks significantly better than previous models (e.g., GPT-4).
A key feature of these models is "test-time compute," which allows the AI to spend more computational resources during the inference phase (when answering questions), enabling it to think more thoroughly. This is demonstrated with an example where the 01 model walks through a cipher decoding problem, in a manner reminiscent of a human solving a puzzle.
The video notes that access to the "hidden chain of thought" is restricted, preventing others from replicating the results by using this hidden information as synthetic training data.
"...these reasoning models have been known by many many different names in the past. In the beginning we called them qar that was the code name of the project later they were called strawberry. Now of course they're being referred to as the 01 the 03..."
Chinese Replication Efforts & Open Sourcing:
The video focuses on a recent paper from Fudan University Shanghai AI laboratory titled "Scaling of Search and Learning: A Road Map to Reproduce o1" which explicitly lays out a method for reproducing OpenAI's 01 model using reinforcement learning techniques.
The video presenter, Wes Roth, speculates this publication indicates that the secret behind OpenAI's models may have been cracked by Chinese researchers. He believes this to be a major development in the AI space.
The video notes an irony of the situation, that China seems to be taking a lot of technology from OpenAI, using it to build the models, then releasing them as open-source, a goal of OpenAI's mission which has been somewhat abandoned.
Key Techniques:
Reinforcement Learning: The video emphasizes the importance of reinforcement learning in training reasoning models. It mentions the core components: policy initialization, reward design, search, and learning. Reinforcement learning is explained using a dog training analogy, rewards (positive reinforcement) and penalties (negative reinforcement).
Knowledge Distillation: This technique is explained as using the outputs of a large, powerful "teacher" model to train a smaller, more efficient "student" model. The student model often retains many of the abilities of the teacher model, without the computational expense. The presenter cites Microsoft's Orca paper as a prime example. It is pointed out that models like Gro and DeepSeek often falsely claim to be GPT-4, due to having been trained using GPT-4 outputs.
Iterative Bootstrapping: The video explains how models are capable of improving their accuracy by creating their own training data based on the results of the reasoning capabilities of previous models. This, it is stated, could lead models to improve past human level intelligence.
Search & Test Time Compute: The video emphasizes that by using the 'search' functionality, models are able to arrive at answers in a way that is very different from non-reasoning models. A key concept here is test time compute, where the AI model is allowed to use extensive computation during the inference/question answering phase, allowing it to explore the solution space more fully. It gives a detailed example of how the 01 model goes through several possibilities in a step-by-step manner.
"...they're saying that with search you know that data generated by search can be used to improve policy improve better performance and they're referring to that as learning so here I guess the sort of the search would be it generating the answers right and the learning would be the fine-tuning and kind of like refining that uh process."
Reward Systems & Dense vs. Sparse Rewards:
The video differentiates between "outcome rewards" (rewarding only the final result) and "process rewards" (rewarding intermediate steps). The video suggests that process rewards offer better guidance, although they are more difficult to implement (often involving human annotation). It explains that granular rewards that occur often are more effective in guiding the model in a correct direction than large rewards that are few and far between. An example is given of two AI robots playing hide and seek.
The video highlights that reward modelling is essential for pushing current AI models towards the next stages of development.
The Five Stages of AGI: * OpenAI's five-stage roadmap to AGI is referenced. Stage 1 is chat bots, stage 2 is reasoners, stage 3 is agents, stage 4 is innovators, and stage 5 is organizations. The 01 model is described as having reached stage 2, and the next move is towards stage 3.
"..level one are chat Bots the eyes with conversational language so this is gbt 4 pretty much everything below it and you know gbt 40 up to gbt 40 all those things can be thought of as level one AIS right and level two are reasoners human level problem solvers..."
Implications and Open Questions:
The video raises the question of whether the open-sourcing of these powerful AI models is a net positive, given potential safety concerns. It asks whether there is a threshold where open-sourcing becomes too dangerous, or if the benefits outweigh the risks.
It poses a question if the fact that China is making this technology open source is a good thing for the world or not.
III. Key Quotes
"I'm going to say it I did not see this one coming I don't know if anyone saw this one coming..." (Describing the unexpected speed of AI advancement)
"open is threatening to ban users for asking strawberry about its reasoning additional violations of this policy may result in a loss of access to GPT 40 with reasoning..." (Highlighting the secrecy around OpenAI's models)
"...with the 01 Model A lot of this stuff became kind of easy for it because it could kind of sit there and think through it step by step if it ran into an issue..." (Describing the reasoning ability of these advanced models)
"...they're taking the big reasoning model they have they they create that training data for it using its reasoning they do post training of this model with that data and all of a sudden this model does extremely well..." (Describing the knowledge distillation approach taken by DeepSeek.)
"...the key to extending A1 to real world environments lies in reward modeling..." (Emphasizing the importance of reward systems).
IV. Conclusion
The video suggests that the rapid advancements in AI, specifically in the development of reasoning models and their replication by Chinese researchers, could lead to a significant paradigm shift. The video also suggests that the open-source approach taken by Chinese researchers represents an interesting dynamic shift away from the closed system approach by OpenAI, and it is not yet clear what the long-term implications will be. The presenter closes by saying the speed and type of advancements in the field have not necessarily been what was expected, and asks the audience what they think, specifically concerning whether open-sourcing this technology is a good idea.
This briefing document captures the essential points of the video transcript and will be helpful in understanding the context of recent AI developments.
